items.name: The Captain of Köpenick
clues: A town just outside Berlin (today part of the city), 16 October 1906.
A shoemaker with a criminal record decided that people would do anything for a man in the right clothes.
He bought pieces of an army captain's uniform second-hand, then ordered about ten real soldiers to follow him, and they did.
They occupied the town hall, arrested the mayor and took just over 4,000 marks. Ten days later he was caught, and he was sentenced to four years in prison.
The Kaiser himself pardoned him in 1908, and he became a celebrity. A famous play about him appeared in 1931.
Today a statue of him in uniform stands outside the town hall, and Germans still call a cheeky trick like this a “Köpenickiade”.

items.name: Milli Vanilli
clues: Munich, 1988. A German record producer put together a new pop act.
Two young dancers with great looks and even better hair would be the faces of the music.
The voices on the records belonged to other studio singers. The two stars only moved their lips.
In July 1989, at a live show in the United States, the backing track jumped and kept repeating the same line.
In 1990 they won a Grammy for Best New Artist. Once the producer admitted the truth, the award was taken away.
Their biggest hit was “Girl You Know It's True”, and their name sounds like a flavour of ice cream.

items.name: Theranos
clues: Silicon Valley, 2003. A 19-year-old Stanford student started a company, and soon dropped out to run it.
A whole range of medical tests from just a few drops of blood from your finger, cheaper and faster than any lab.
Its own machines didn't work as promised, so many tests were quietly run on ordinary machines made by other companies.
In 2015 the Wall Street Journal published an investigation into whether its tests really worked.
In 2022 the founder was found guilty of fraud and sentenced to more than eleven years in prison.
Its founder wore black polo necks like Steve Jobs, and the TV series about her is called The Dropout.

items.name: Fyre Festival
clues: The Bahamas, April 2017.
A luxury music festival on a Caribbean island, with villas, gourmet food and celebrities.
Famous models promoted it on Instagram by all posting the same plain orange square.
Guests arrived to find disaster-relief tents instead of villas, and a cheese sandwich in a polystyrene box.
In 2018 the organiser was sentenced to six years in prison for fraud.
In 2019 two documentaries about it came out at almost the same time. Its name is an unusual spelling of something hot.

items.name: Anna Delvey
clues: New York, 2013 to 2017.
A young woman told everyone she was a German heiress with a fortune of around €60 million waiting for her abroad, and planned a private art club for the rich.
She lived in expensive hotels, left bills unpaid and applied to banks for a $22 million loan.
The unpaid bills piled up, and in 2017 she was arrested.
In 2019 she was sentenced to four to twelve years. She was really born near Moscow and grew up in a small town in North Rhine-Westphalia.
In 2022 Netflix told her story in a series called Inventing Anna.

items.name: Dieselgate
clues: The United States first, then the rest of the world. It became public in September 2015.
A big carmaker sold its diesel cars as clean, eco-friendly and cheap to run.
Secret software noticed when a car was being tested and only then switched the full emissions controls on. On the road, some cars produced up to 40 times the legal limit of nitrogen oxides.
A small university lab in West Virginia tested the cars on real roads and found the numbers didn't match.
About 11 million cars worldwide were affected, the chief executive resigned and the company paid more than $30 billion in fines and settlements.
The scandal is named after the fuel, plus the ending of a famous American political scandal of the 1970s.
